title: George Rogers Clark
summary: George Rogers Clark staged at Corn Island in the Falls of the Ohio in 1778 before his Illinois Campaign, and the settlement he left became Louisville.
bodyMarkdown:
[George Rogers Clark](https://grokipedia.com/page/George_Rogers_Clark) was born on November 19, 1752, in Albemarle County, Virginia, and came west as a surveyor in the early 1770s. He served as a militia captain on the Kentucky frontier, and by 1777 the Kentucky stations were under constant pressure. Native nations allied with the British at Detroit were raiding the settlements, fighting to keep settlers out of their hunting grounds.

Clark's answer was to strike at the source. On January 2, 1778, Virginia governor Patrick Henry gave him secret orders to raise men and move against British posts in the Illinois country. Clark gathered his force at Corn Island, a small island at the [Falls of the Ohio](/stories/falls-of-the-ohio/).

On June 24, 1778, during a solar eclipse, about 175 men shot the rapids and headed downriver. On July 4 they took [Kaskaskia](https://grokipedia.com/page/Kaskaskia,_Illinois) without a fight. Clark won the French inhabitants over as allies, and Cahokia followed (see [Illinois Confederation at Cahokia](/stories/illinois-confederation-at-cahokia/)). When British lieutenant governor [Henry Hamilton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Henry_Hamilton_(colonial_administrator)) retook Vincennes, Clark led a grueling 240-mile winter march through flooded country and forced Hamilton's surrender on February 25, 1779, in the [Siege of Fort Vincennes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Siege_of_Fort_Vincennes).

The families who had come downriver with Clark built the town he left behind. According to [a history of Corn Island](https://grokipedia.com/page/corn_island_(kentucky)), about sixty civilians first settled on the island in 1778. In 1779 they moved to the Kentucky shore and named their town for France's [Louis XVI](https://grokipedia.com/page/Louis_XVI), and Virginia chartered [Louisville](https://grokipedia.com/page/Louisville,_Kentucky) on May 1, 1780. In 1781 Clark's troops built [Fort Nelson](https://grokipedia.com/page/fort_nelson_(kentucky)) on the mainland, and it served as his western headquarters.

Clark's war had another side. In 1780 and 1782 he led campaigns into the Shawnee homeland north of the Ohio, burning towns and cornfields, the second in reprisal for the defeat at [Blue Licks](/stories/battle-of-blue-licks/). To Kentucky settlers he was a protector; to the Shawnee these were attacks on their families and food supplies in a war over their own land (see [Shawnee Chillicothe Divisions](/stories/shawnee-chillicothe-divisions/)). Historians continue to weigh both views.

Clark's later years were hard. Virginia's [failure](https://grokipedia.com/page/George_Rogers_Clark) to fully repay his campaign expenses left him with personal debts and forced the sale of his lands. A stroke in 1809 cost him a leg, and he died on February 13, 1818, at Locust Grove near Louisville.

## Kentucky today

Clark was first buried at Locust Grove, and in 1869 his remains were moved to [Cave Hill Cemetery](https://grokipedia.com/page/Cave_Hill_Cemetery) in Louisville, where a monument marks his grave. [Historic Locust Grove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locust_Grove_(Louisville,_Kentucky)) still stands, and a granite monument in Fort Nelson Park downtown marks the [fort](https://grokipedia.com/page/fort_nelson_(kentucky)). Across the river, [Falls of the Ohio State Park](https://grokipedia.com/page/Falls_of_the_Ohio_State_Park) protects the rapids his men ran in 1778.
